title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 216: Bioprospecting in the Cryosphere
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 216 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

Bioprospecting in the Cryosphere: The Cold Search for Novel Antibiotics

Paragraph 1. Modern medicine is entering a dangerous crisis. Decades of antibiotic overuse in hospitals and livestock farming have created drug-resistant germs known as 'superbugs'. The World Health Organization estimates that unless new medicines appear soon, resistant infections could kill ten million people every year by 2050. Historically, almost all antibiotics came from bacteria living in farm soil, yet after seventy years of searching, researchers mostly find the same old molecules again.

Paragraph 2. To escape this dead end, scientists are exploring frozen regions of Earth—glaciers, underground polar lakes, and frozen Antarctic earth. Far from empty ice, these freezing worlds hold cold-adapted microbes called psychrophiles. Chemical biologist Dr. Rebecca Frost notes that surviving extreme cold, strong ultraviolet light, and scarce food forced these bacteria to build flexible cell membranes and active enzymes that work smoothly near freezing point. To defeat rival microbes in tiny ice spaces, they also produce natural germ-killing chemicals never seen before in medicine.

Paragraph 3. Searching for these hidden drugs, microbiologist Dr. Liam Chen led a team deep into Greenland. His expedition drilled four hundred metres down to pull out 30,000-year-old ice cores and isolated over two hundred bacterial strains. In lab trials, a compound taken from a newly discovered bacterium destroyed MRSA—a dangerous hospital superbug—by breaking apart the protective shield that normally blocks standard antibiotics.

Paragraph 4. Turning polar discoveries into factory-made pills remains difficult, however. Industrial engineer Dr. Sven Lindholm warns that standard drug tanks are built for warm bacteria, whereas cold microbes die once broth temperatures rise above ten degrees Celsius. Cooling huge factory tanks is terribly expensive unless scientists move the cold-germ genes into warm-tolerant host cells.

Paragraph 5. Legal and climate problems add further urgency. Bioethicist Dr. Maya Patel points out that the 1959 Antarctic treaty covers peace and nature protection, yet says nothing about who owns profits from polar drug discoveries. Without clear international rules, private companies might take huge profits without supporting polar conservation. Meanwhile, rapid glacier melting threatens to wipe out thousands of valuable ice microbes before researchers can even record them.

q1.text: Using too many antibiotics in medicine and farming helped create resistant superbugs.

steps: Đoạn 1: Lạm dụng ở bệnh viện và chăn nuôi gia súc đã tạo ra siêu vi khuẩn kháng thuốc.

q2.text: Ordinary agricultural soil continues to supply plenty of brand-new antibiotic structures.

steps: Đoạn 1: Các nhà nghiên cứu chủ yếu chỉ tìm lại được những phân tử cũ.

q3.text: Dr. Rebecca Frost personally joined Dr. Chen's drilling team in Greenland.

steps: Đoạn 2 & 3: Bài không nói Dr. Frost có tham gia chuyến khoan băng ở Greenland cùng Dr. Chen hay không.

q4.text: Standard factory fermentation equipment is already designed to handle freezing microbes cheaply.

steps: Đoạn 4: Thiết bị chuẩn chỉ dành cho vi khuẩn ưa ấm; làm lạnh bồn chứa rất đắt đỏ.

q5.text: Global warming could destroy undiscovered polar microbes before science studies them.

steps: Đoạn 5: Băng tan nhanh đe dọa xóa sổ hàng ngàn vi sinh vật trước khi kịp ghi nhận.
Đoạn 4: "...when broth temperatures rise above ten degrees..."
